person.headline: Building AI products that work in production. Open source since 2016, research since 2017, shipping since 2019.

about.thesis: I build the full stack around the model — the product layer that compensates for what the model can't do on its own. Prompt design as defensive programming. Context management as infrastructure. Evaluation as a first-class concern, not an afterthought. The customer interacts with the product, not the model, and that distinction drives every design decision I make.
about.arc: I started contributing to open source in 2016, published research and filed patents starting in 2017, built my first ML product in 2019, and have been shipping enterprise AI products since. Before AI, I spent 18 years designing internal developer platforms at scale — CI/CD, test automation, defect tracking, measurement frameworks. Every integration problem I solved in platform engineering showed up again when AI arrived. The scars transferred.
about.looking_for: AI product management and strategy roles where AI is the core business, not a bolt-on feature — teams that need someone who understands both the model's capabilities and the enterprise constraints that determine whether it actually ships.

beliefs.statement: Builders have more credibility than commentators.
beliefs.detail: Ship it. Then talk about it. The order matters.

beliefs.statement: The customer interacts with the product, not the model.
beliefs.detail: The product exists to compensate for the model's weaknesses. I build the full stack around the model.

beliefs.statement: Prompts are interfaces to stochastic functions.
beliefs.detail: Defensive programming for AI. Account for what the model might get wrong, not just what it should get right.

beliefs.statement: Quality is a platform problem, not a testing problem.
beliefs.detail: 18 years of IDP taught me that quality is designed into systems, not inspected into products.
Prove it works at limited scope with measurable targets first, then scale. Trust is earned incrementally.

beliefs.statement: Create your own frameworks. Don't just use others'.
beliefs.detail: TAQi for test automation. HMF for career navigation. CricketBench for model evaluation. Original thinking compounds.

beliefs.statement: Connection is the one thing AI can't replicate.
beliefs.detail: I coined 'Connecticate' — the ability to connect while you communicate. That's the human edge.

beliefs.statement: Accidents, luck, and detours deserve gratitude.
beliefs.detail: The path from Chennai to Dallas, from telecom to AI, was never a straight line. Every detour built something.

projects.name: Agent Interpretability Tool
projects.one_liner: What's actually happening under the hood in a coding agent — made visible.
projects.problem: Coding agents make dozens of decisions per session: which files to read, which tools to call, how to decompose a task, when to backtrack. By default, all of that is invisible. You see the output and hope it's right.
projects.what_it_does: Surfaces the agent's decision trace — tool calls, context selection, branching decisions, failure points — as a legible product feature, not a research artifact.
projects.why_it_matters: If you can't explain what an agent did and why, you can't debug it, trust it, or improve it. Enterprise buyers won't adopt what they can't audit.
projects.what_i_learned: Interpretability isn't a research luxury — it's a product requirement. The target user is a team lead deciding whether to trust an agent's output, not an ML researcher.

projects.name: Context Management System
projects.one_liner: General-purpose infrastructure for managing what an AI system knows, keeps, and forgets — and why.
projects.problem: Context is the scarcest resource in any LLM-based system. Every token in the window has a cost, and most systems waste it — stuffing irrelevant history, losing critical state, or treating context as a FIFO queue when the problem demands something smarter.
projects.what_it_does: Infrastructure for managing context across AI system interactions — what goes in, what stays, what gets evicted, and why. Built as general-purpose, not tied to a single application.
projects.why_it_matters: Most teams bolt on context management after the prototype works. By then, the architecture fights you. This treats context as first-class infrastructure from the start.
projects.what_i_learned: Context management is where product intuition and systems engineering intersect. Get it wrong and the model looks broken — hallucinations, lost threads, repeated questions. Get it right and nobody notices, which is the point.

projects.name: Metabolistic Storyteller
projects.one_liner: Traditional ML product — where the AI product journey started.
projects.why_it_matters: First experience taking a model from notebook to product. The lesson that stuck: the model is 20% of the work. Data pipelines, evaluation, edge case handling, and the interface the user actually touches — that's the other 80%.
projects.what_i_learned: Built in 2019, before LLMs were accessible. The constraints of traditional ML — feature engineering by hand, smaller models, no pretrained language understanding — made the product layer do more work. That discipline carries forward.

projects.name: Code Review Bot
projects.one_liner: Automated code review tool built in the pre-LLM era.
projects.problem: Code review was a bottleneck. Needed automation using the tools available at the time — no transformers, no API calls.
projects.what_it_does: Pattern matching, heuristics, and a deep understanding of what reviewers actually look for. Solved a real workflow problem without modern LLM capabilities.
projects.why_it_matters: Solved a real workflow problem using the tools available at the time. Proved that automation doesn't need the latest model — it needs the right constraints.
projects.what_i_learned: The constraints of pre-LLM automation made the value of LLMs concrete later. Knowing what was hard before makes you a better judge of what's easy now.

projects.name: CricketMind
projects.one_liner: Fine-tuned NVIDIA Nemotron-Mini-4B for cricket domain expertise. 67.5% vs 30.2% baseline.
projects.problem: No existing LLM understood cricket deeply enough — the Laws, the strategy, the edge cases. Domain adaptation shouldn't need massive budgets.
projects.what_it_does: QLoRA fine-tuning with response distillation using Claude as teacher model. Custom CricketBench evaluation suite with 25 questions across 4 categories. Runs on $5 of RunPod A100 compute.
projects.why_it_matters: Proves that domain-adapted LLMs don't need massive budgets. Evaluation-driven training: built the benchmark first, then trained to beat it.
projects.what_i_learned: The benchmark defined the goal, not the other way around. Evaluation-first is how you avoid fooling yourself that the model improved.
projects.architecture_notes: Teacher model (Claude) generates reference answers -> QLoRA fine-tuning on Nemotron-Mini-4B -> CricketBench evaluation loop
projects.results: 67.5% accuracy on CricketBench vs 30.2% baseline. $5 total compute cost.

projects.name: BTCExpert / CIAL
projects.one_liner: Crypto intelligence platform with real-time streaming and semantic search.
projects.what_it_does: FastAPI backend, TimescaleDB for time-series, Kafka for event streaming, pgvector for semantic search, Redis caching, WebSocket streaming handling 10K+ concurrent connections. Full observability stack.
projects.architecture_notes: Kafka ingestion -> TimescaleDB storage -> pgvector semantic index -> FastAPI serving -> WebSocket real-time push

projects.name: GlucoLens
projects.one_liner: Health monitoring using causal discovery — not just correlations, actual causal relationships.
projects.problem: Most health analytics find correlations and present them as insights. Correlation is not causation, and in health data the distinction matters.
projects.what_it_does: Uses PCMCI for causal discovery and STUMPY for pattern detection in health time-series data. Identifies actual causal relationships between variables.
projects.why_it_matters: Moving beyond correlations in health data. Finding what actually causes what, not just what co-occurs.
projects.architecture_notes: Health data ingestion -> STUMPY pattern detection -> PCMCI causal graph construction -> causal relationship reporting

projects.name: Code-RAG
projects.one_liner: Local RAG-based code assistant that runs fully offline.
projects.problem: Code search and assistance shouldn't require sending proprietary code to external APIs.
projects.what_it_does: Vector indexing of codebases, semantic search, retrieval tuning — all local. No external API calls. Built from scratch to prove upstream intervention matters more than retrieval algorithm choice.
projects.why_it_matters: Proves that preprocessing and source quality beats retrieval tuning. The RAG Upstream Intervention thesis in practice.
projects.architecture_notes: Local codebase indexing -> vector embedding -> semantic retrieval -> context assembly -> local LLM generation

projects.name: Kafka Stream Transformer
projects.one_liner: Real-time Kafka microservice with live WebSocket dashboard.
projects.what_it_does: Event streaming and transformation at scale with built-in real-time observability via WebSocket dashboard.
projects.architecture_notes: Kafka consumer -> stream transformation -> WebSocket push -> live dashboard

projects.name: Review Buddy
projects.one_liner: GitHub App that assigns code reviewers based on file ownership history.
projects.problem: Manual reviewer assignment is slow and often misses the person who actually knows the code.
projects.what_it_does: Analyzes git blame and file ownership patterns to intelligently assign the right reviewer for each PR.
projects.why_it_matters: Developer experience problem solved with data already in the repo. No ML needed — just smart use of git history.

now._description: Where my head is at right now. Updated periodically.

items.detail: Deep-diving into how MCP solves the MxN integration problem I fought for 18 years. Writing a 3-part series connecting my LlamaIndex PR experience to the MCP philosophy.
Proving that domain-adapted LLMs don't need massive budgets. CricketMind runs on $5 of compute. Exploring QLoRA, response distillation, and evaluation-driven training loops.
Moving beyond correlations with PCMCI and STUMPY. Building GlucoLens to find real causal relationships, not just patterns that look convincing.
Mapping the 8 layers from data to deployment to observability. Most teams only see 2-3 layers. Writing to make the full stack visible.
Upstream intervention over retrieval tuning. Preprocessing and source quality matter more than the retrieval algorithm. Building Code-RAG to prove it.
Publishing consistently across Substack and Medium. Turning 24+ drafts into finished pieces. The act of writing is how I learn.
